text: SciTaRC: Benchmarking QA on Scientific Tabular Data that Requires Language Reasoning and Complex Computation Hexuan Wang Yaxuan Ren Srikar Bommireddypalli Shuxian Chen hwang302@jh.edu yren46@jh.edu sbommir1@jh.edu schen354@jh.edu Adarsh Prabhudesai Rongkun Zhou Elina Baral Philipp Koehn aprabhu3@jh.edu rzhou33@jh.edu ebaral1@jhu.edu phi@jhu.edu Center for Language and Speech Processing Johns Hopkins University Baltimore, Maryland, USA Abstract We introduce SciTaRC, an expert-authored benchmark of questions about tabular data in scientific papers requiring both deep language reasoning and complex computation. We show that current state-of-the-art AI models fail on at least 23% of these questions, a gap that re- mains significant even for highly capable open- weight models like Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, which fails on 65.5% of the tasks. Our analy- sis reveals a universal “execution bottleneck”: both code and language models struggle to faithfully execute plans, even when provided with correct strategies. Specifically, code-based methods prove brittle on raw scientific tables, while natural language reasoning primarily fails due to initial comprehension issues and calcu- lation errors. 1 1 Introduction The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have advanced from knowledge recall and simple inference to more complex problem solving that requires multi-step reasoning (Naveed et al., 2024; Ferrag et al., 2025). However, there are still types of computation where traditional computer science algorithms are superior, particularly tasks requiring long-horizon execution, precise intermediate com- putation, or strict control flow (Plaat et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b). This observation motivates hy- brid approaches that combine neural and symbolic reasoning, an idea that also underlies recent work on agentic AI systems (Wan et al., 2024; Colelough and Regli, 2025). Scientific tables provide a natural stress test for such hybrid reasoning. To benchmark current AI system performance on such challenges, we manually created a set of sci- entific tabular reasoning questions. While designed to be self-contained, these tasks demand deep lan- guage understanding, strategic planning, and com- plex calculation. Each instance consists of a ques- tion, one or more tables, a pseudo-code execution plan, a gold response, and an automatic evaluation protocol. In contrast to other recently proposed ta- ble QA benchmarks, our questions are authored by domain experts and not automatically generated by an LLM. Figure 1 illustrates a representative example. Despite recent advances, current state-of- 1 arXiv:2603.08910v1 [cs.CL] 9 Mar 2026 the-art models like GPT-5 only achieve an accuracy score of 76.8% on this benchmark, highlighting the need to develop better methods. In this paper, we detail the construction of the SciTaRC benchmark, evaluate a wide range of pro- prietary and open-weight models, and analyze the factors that drive model success and failure. Our analysis reveals several key findings: (1) reasoning- optimized models outperform larger baselines but still fail on a non-trivial subset of problems; (2) fail- ures arise primarily from question comprehension, but also during computations; (3) program-based reasoning underperforms natural language reason- ing in zero-shot settings due to brittleness in han- dling heterogeneous scientific tables; and (4) sepa- rating planning from execution shows that execu- tion compliance, rather than strategy formation, is the dominant failure mode. These results suggest that improving faithful execution over structured data remains a central challenge for future agentic and neuro-symbolic systems. 2 2 Related Work Table QA Benchmarks. Early benchmarks such as WikiTableQuestions (Pasupat and Liang, 2015) and TabFact (Chen et al., 2020) focused on clean Wikipedia tables with simple reasoning patterns. Recent work has pushed toward greater complexity: TableEval (Zhu et al., 2025) emphasizes messy real- world tables, TQA-Bench (Qiu et al., 2024) targets multi-table relational reasoning, and TableBench (Wu et al., 2025a) aggregates diverse analytical tasks. SCITAT (Zhang et al., 2025) also ad- dresses scientific tables but focuses on table-text integration rather than computational complexity. Domain-specific datasets include AIT-QA (Katsis et al., 2022) for airline finance, HiTab (Cheng et al., 2022) for hierarchical

multi-table relational reasoning, and TableBench (Wu et al., 2025a) aggregates diverse analytical tasks. SCITAT (Zhang et al., 2025) also ad- dresses scientific tables but focuses on table-text integration rather than computational complexity. Domain-specific datasets include AIT-QA (Katsis et al., 2022) for airline finance, HiTab (Cheng et al., 2022) for hierarchical structures, and WikiMixQA (Foroutan et al., 2025) for multimodal reasoning. However, these benchmarks lack the combination of scientific domain conventions, explicit algorith- mic plans, and quantifiable complexity metrics that SciTaRC provides. Moreover, many existing datasets rely heavily on automatic generation or templated question–answer construction, whereas SciTaRC is fully authored and reviewed by domain experts. Reasoning Methods and Diagnostics. Recent surveys (Fang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b) high- 2Dataset and Evaluation Protocol is available at light persistent challenges in table understanding. Diagnostic studies reveal specific weaknesses: Sui et al. (2024) shows sensitivity to serialization for- mats, and Akhtar et al. (2023) demonstrate in- consistency in numerical reasoning. Methodologi- cal advances include multi-agent frameworks (Bai et al., 2025; Ma, 2025), specialized reasoning ar- chitectures (Xiong et al., 2025), and inference-time scaling (Yang et al., 2025b). SciTaRC comple- ments these by providing complexity metrics that quantify reasoning demands, a diagnostic test set for evaluating emerging methods, and systematic analysis of LLM behavior and failure modes on scientific tables. Neuro-Symbolic Approaches. Program-based reasoning methods like Program-of-Thought (Chen et al., 2023) and PAL (Gao et al., 2023) generate executable code to disentangle computation from reasoning. DACO (Wu et al., 2024) advances code- based data analysis, while recent work explores LLM-symbolic integration (Kulkarni et al., 2025). Despite these advances, questions remain about whether program-based methods can handle the heterogeneous structures of scientific tables in zero- shot settings. SciTaRC addresses this through man- ually written pseudo-code plans that enable sys- tematic decomposition of planning failures versus execution failures—a distinction not possible with existing benchmarks. 3 Dataset Our dataset is based on scientific papers sourced from recent arXiv preprints, mainly in the domain of artificial intelligence. We downloaded the La- TeX sources for these papers, and consolidated them into a single file. 3.1 Question Creation For each paper, a question author selected 1 to 3 tables, wrote out a question and the correspond- ing answer. The tables were then automatically extracted from the LaTeX file and added to the dataset. The dataset consists of the following fields: • arXiv paper ID • question (text) • answer

each paper, a question author selected 1 to 3 tables, wrote out a question and the correspond- ing answer. The tables were then automatically extracted from the LaTeX file and added to the dataset. The dataset consists of the following fields: • arXiv paper ID • question (text) • answer (text) • LaTeX source of each relevant table • LaTeX sources of all tables in the paper • LaTeX source of the full paper 2 The question creators (all authors of this paper) comprise undergraduate, Masters, and PhD stu- dents as well as a professor working in the area of natural language processing. The questions were designed to be answerable unambiguously just given the tables (with captions) and general domain knowledge about the subject matter. Each question was checked by two reviewers (different from the creator). Some of the questions were too complex to come up manually with the correct gold answer. In those cases, a short script was written to compute correct results. These scripts were very ad-hoc and written in a mix of programming languages, so we do not include them as part of the released dataset. 3.2 Evaluation Protocol Since the answers are free-form, with a mix of text and numbers, sometimes consisting of multiple items, matching answers generated by a model with the gold answer is non-trivial. For example, for the example question in Fig- ure 1, the correct answer is: Korean; different for GPT-4o-mini-Audio (Cantonese) and GPT-4o-mini (Russian) but an AI system may respond The hardest language for Qwen2-Audio is Korean. For GPT-4o-mini-Audio, the hardest language is Cantonese. For GPT- 4o-mini, the hardest language is Russian. Hence, we created an evaluation protocol that uses a large language model to perform the match- ing (LLM as judge) (Zheng et al., 2023). This protocol uses Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and prompts it with the question, the answer of the automatic system, and the gold an- swer. The exact prompt is detailed in Appendix A. To validate the reliability of this automatic eval- uation, we conducted a manual annotation on a subset of 245 questions. We compared the auto- matic evaluator’s decisions against human judg- ments for answers generated by GPT-4o (OpenAI et al., 2024) and Llama-3-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024). We found a high degree of agreement, with an alignment rate of 97.6% for GPT-4o and 95.5% for Llama-3-8B-Instruct. 3.3 Pseudo Code Plans As additional annotation

If multiple values are used concurrently, explicit variable names are used. 3.4 Quantifying Complexity To get a better understanding of the challenges of SciTaRC, we define metrics characterizing diffi- culty along two dimensions: Input Complexity. We measure the amount of information to be processed: • Context Load (Stok): Total token count of seri- alized tables, measuring context length. • Structural Size (Scell): Total grid cells (in- cluding empty) parsed from LaTex, representing amount of data items. • Input Scope (Stab): Number of distinct tables required, measuring cross-table linking needs. 3 Model Family Model Name Method Size Acc. We quantify algorith- mic hardness via ground-truth plans: • Calculation Intensity (Icalc): Count of COMPUTE operations, measuring arithmetic burden. • Retrieval Demand (Iretr): Count of SELECT op- erations, measuring retrieval frequency. • Plan Horizon (Lplan): Total instruction count, serving as a proxy for reasoning depth. • Control Flow (Cflow): Composite score Cflow = Nloop + Nif + Dmax, where Nloop and Nif count iterative and conditional blocks, and Dmax represents maximum nesting depth. 4 Benchmarking State-of-the-Art 4.1 Experimental Setup We evaluate 24 distinct models spanning two pri- mary categories: Proprietary Frontier Models (e.g., GPT-5, Grok-4.1) and Open-Weight Models. The latter includes both leading generalist models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025b), Llama 3.3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen 3 (Yang et al., 2025a)) and code-optimized specialists (e.g., Qwen-Coder (Hui et al., 2024)). We employ two zero-shot prompting paradigms tailored to the strengths of each model: • Chain-of-Thought (CoT): For the majority of generalist models, we use a standard zero-shot prompt (Wei et al., 2023; Kojima et al., 2023) encouraging step-by-step natural language rea- soning. • Program-of-Thought (PoT): For code- optimized models and select generalist models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2, Claude 4.5 Sonnet), we instruct the model to generate executable Python code (Chen et al., 2023) to derive the answer. To visualize the consistency of these behaviors, Figure 3 breaks down agree- ment at the question level. While stronger models generally achieve higher overall accuracy, their ca- pabilities are not a strict superset of weaker models. We observe frequent instances where smaller mod- els successfully solve “hard” questions that frontier models miss, indicating that difficulty is often de- termined by specific architectural fits rather than scale alone. We observe three primary trends that character- ize scientific table reasoning: Reasoning Strategies Amplify Capabilities. Models trained with reinforcement learn- ing (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025a) for reasoning significantly boost performance, enabling models to outperform larger standard baselines. For instance, Kimi-K2-Thinking (73.3%) exceeds its base model Kimi-K2 (49.1%) by over 24 percent- age points. This capability allows efficient scaling: the 32B DeepSeek-R1-Distill reasoning model (41.5%) scores higher than the 71B Llama-3.3 model (34.5%). Model Scale Matters, but Capabilities Vary. While larger models generally perform better, the improvement is not strictly linear. As shown in Figure 3, smaller or weaker models occasionally solve "hard" questions that frontier models miss. This stochasticity suggests that reasoning is not a single monotonic skill; different architectures may find different types of logic easier, even if they lack overall capacity. We focus on two dimensions: the scale of the input data and the complexity of the required reasoning. Input Scale Exposes Fragility. As illustrated in Figure 4, performance generally degrades as the structural size of the table (Scell) increases. This downward trend is consistent across both nat- ural language (CoT) and code generation (PoT) paradigms. However, the data reveals a sharp di- vide in model robustness. Frontier models exhibit remarkable stability: Grok-4 (+0.1%) and DS-V3 (-2.0%) maintain its accuracy even as tables ex- ceed 400 cells. In contrast, smaller models suffer catastrophic collapse due to context pressure, with Gemma-3-27B dropping by 41.4 percentage points. We observe similar patterns for Context Load (Stok) and Input Scope (Stab), which are detailed in Ap- pendix C. Impact of Reasoning Complexity. Beyond data scale, we examine how the algorithmic require- ments of the question affect performance (Figure 5). We observe a consistent negative trend across all metrics, but the drivers of failure differ. • Plan Horizon is a Universal Bottleneck (Lplan): Multi-step reasoning prove uniquely difficult for all systems. Even robust frontier models like DeepSeek-V3.2 (thinking) drop by 13.4% when moving to long-horizon questions, and the aver- age system degrades by 25.2% to 35.5% depend-

Even robust frontier models like DeepSeek-V3.2 (thinking) drop by 13.4% when moving to long-horizon questions, and the aver- age system degrades by 25.2% to 35.5% depend- ing on the method (CoT or PoT). This suggests that maintaining execution fidelity across long sequences remains a persistent challenge across the board. • Code Generation Degrades with Complex- ity (Icalc): Contrary to the expectation that code handles math better, Program-of-Thought (PoT) degrades faster than natural language on calculation-heavy tasks. PoT accuracy drops by 29.8% (vs 23.2% for CoT), likely because gener- ating the correct syntax for long operation chains zero-shot is more prone to error than natural lan- guage reasoning. • Complex Logic Separates Reasoning Models (Cflow): Questions with nested loops or condi- tionals reveal a stark divergence. While standard models like GPT-4o suffer significant degrada- tion (-29.5%), reasoning-optimized models like Kimi-Thinking and DeepSeek-V3.2 remain re- markably robust (exhibiting changes of +0.9% and -2.6% respectively), indicating that their spe- cific training enables them to handle structural logic that confuses generalist models. 5 Disentangling Reasoning: The Planning Ablation Motivated by the algorithmic barriers identified in Section 4.3, we investigate whether model failure stems from flawed strategy formulation (planning) or flawed stepwise implementation (execution). Figure 7 and Table 2 illustrate a distinct capability trade-off. Explicit planning significantly aids the code- specialized Qwen-Coder, yielding accuracy gains of +1.9% with autonomous planning and +6.2% when provided with an oracle plan, confirming that structured blueprints reduce error in programmatic generation. Conversely, generalist language mod- els consistently regress (-5.4% to -10.0%). This di- vergence highlights a Compliance Cost: the over- head of strictly following a rigid script outweighs its benefit for models whose intrinsic reasoning already suffices on simpler tasks. Moreover, pro- viding an Oracle plan does not guarantee improved accuracy over an autonomously generated plan for larger model, suggesting that an external strategy must fit the model’s intrinsic reasoning mode to be effective. However, for smaller architectures, the Oracle Plan remains a definitive upper bound on the Gain Curve, revealing a significant latent exe- cution capability that autonomous planning fails to realize. 6 Error Analysis To better understand the “Hard Reasoning Ceil- ing” identified in Section 4.2, we conduct a qual- itative error analysis on 98 failure cases from the outputs of the top-performing open-weight model, DeepSeek-V3.2. We categorize model failures us- ing a four-class error taxonomy designed to isolate where table reasoning breaks. • Comprehension: misunderstanding of the ques- tion

Ceil- ing” identified in Section 4.2, we conduct a qual- itative error analysis on 98 failure cases from the outputs of the top-performing open-weight model, DeepSeek-V3.2. We categorize model failures us- ing a four-class error taxonomy designed to isolate where table reasoning breaks. • Comprehension: misunderstanding of the ques- tion intent, constraints, or the meaning of the table attributes, leading to the wrong objective. • Localization: selecting incorrect rows, columns, Error category Ratio Comprehension 73% Localization 7% Calculation 17% Memory 3% Table 3: Distribution of error categories for DeepSeek- V3.2 across incorrect answer predictions. or values from tables despite a correct objective. • Calculation: producing an incorrect numeric result given the correct evidence and operation. • Memory: failing to retain or consistently apply intermediate results or constraints across steps. Each incorrect prediction is assigned exactly one primary error type based on the earliest point in the reasoning chain at which the output becomes unrecoverable. As shown in Table 3, failures are dominated by Comprehension errors (73%), indicating that DeepSeek-V3.2 most often fails to identify the cor- rect objective from the table and question. Most remaining errors arise from incorrect computations (17%), while localization and memory errors are comparatively rare. We note that comprehension is the first step, and the model may have made subsequent errors which we did not count. 7 Conclusion We presented SciTaRC, a novel expert-authored table QA dataset that stresses language understand- ing, planning, and numerical execution. Despite recent advances, state-of-the-art models fail on over 30% of the benchmark, revealing systematic weaknesses across model families and reasoning paradigms. Our analyses show that these failures 8 arise primarily from errors in comprehension and faithful execution rather than strategy formation. SciTaRC thus highlights execution fidelity as a cen- tral bottleneck for agentic and neuro-symbolic sys- tems, and provides a diagnostic testbed for future methods that aim to bridge this gap. Limitations Dataset Scale and Scope. SciTaRC consists of 370 questions, all of which were human-annotated and double-checked by domain experts. While small compared to automated training corpora, this scale was necessitated by the requirement for rig- orous verification. Consequently, the benchmark is intended as a high-fidelity diagnostic tool rather than a training resource. Additionally, as tables are sourced exclusively from AI-domain arXiv papers, results may not fully generalize to domains with different tabular conventions, such as finance or medicine. Evaluation Protocol. We rely on an LLM-as- a-Judge metric (Llama-3.3-70B).

the benchmark is intended as a high-fidelity diagnostic tool rather than a training resource. Additionally, as tables are sourced exclusively from AI-domain arXiv papers, results may not fully generalize to domains with different tabular conventions, such as finance or medicine. Evaluation Protocol. We rely on an LLM-as- a-Judge metric (Llama-3.3-70B). Although val- idation on a subset of 245 questions showed >95% agreement with human annotators, auto- mated judges lack the rigor of deterministic execu- tion checks and may harbor latent biases, such as inconsistencies in numerical precision or leniency toward semantic equivalence. Reproducibility. Our evaluation includes closed- weight frontier models accessed via opaque APIs. Despite our use of strict generation parameters (e.g., model temperature), these systems are sub- ject to unannounced updates and hidden version changes. This introduces a layer of irreproducibil- ity that does not affect the open-weight models in our leaderboard, where weights are static and inspectable. Planning Constraints. The pseudo-code abla- tion enforces a rigid format in a zero-shot setting. Observed failures may partially stem from the cog- nitive overhead of adhering to this unfamiliar syn- tax (the “Compliance Cost”) rather than a funda- mental inability to reason. Code Execution Robustness. Our Program-of- Thought (PoT) setting operates directly on raw LaTeX without pre-parsed structures. This de- sign choice ensures a strict zero-shot evaluation of the model’s raw capability to handle authentic scientific documents, maintaining fairness across paradigms. However, this approach likely penal- izes code-based strategies, as reasoning failures may be conflated with the brittleness of parsing complex tables from scratch. the evaluation prompt to address three specific scoring challenges in scientific table rea- soning: • Stylistic Invariance: Surface-level variations (e.g., typos, phrasing) are ignored provided the core factual content is accurate. • Numerical Tolerance: To account for round- ing differences, the protocol permits a devia- tion of ±1 in the final significant digit. • Strictness on Extra Information: To avoid rewarding recall bias, the inclusion of unre- quested components not present in the ground truth is penalized. Note on Binarization: While the prompt utilizes a ternary scale (0.0, 0.5, 1.0) to allow the judge to explicitly categorize partial matches, we strictly binarize these scores for the final leaderboard. The ternary structure serves to isolate partially correct answers from the fully correct class; for our re- ported metrics, only a score of 1.0 is treated as a success (1), while 0.5 and 0.0 are treated as failures (0). Consistent with cell count, increasing the token length of the input exerts sig- nificant pressure on weaker models. Qwen3-8B drops by 30.0% and Qwen3-Code by 36.0% when moving from short (< 1k) to long (> 3.3k) con- texts. However, reasoning-optimized frontier mod- els remain immune to this noise, with DeepSeek- V3.2 (+1.5%) and Grok-4.1-R (+1.1%) showing slight performance gains in longer contexts. Input Scope (Stab). Increasing the number of dis- tinct tables (from 1 to 3+) reveals a divergence in capabilities. While typical models degrade, top reasoners like DeepSeek-V3.2 (+13.0%) perform better on multi-table questions. This suggests that strong models possess the reasoning depth to han- dle the structured comparisons in these questions, successfully linking information across disjoint ta- bles where weaker models lose context.
